source: original; documents are public-domain primary sources or paraphrases of them (see each document's sourcing note)
prompt: Evaluate the extent to which African Americans shaped the struggle against slavery in the United States in the period 1800–1848.

documents.title: Gabriel’s rising
documents.source: Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.12 A. Slave Rebellions: Gabriel’s Rebellion.
documents.sourcing: A course-book account of a planned rising by an enslaved Richmond blacksmith, written long after the event.
documents.text: In 1800, Gabriel, an enslaved blacksmith in Richmond, Virginia, planned a rising with as many as a thousand men, hoping to win freedom and a republican government. A heavy rainstorm delayed the march, two enslaved men warned their owners, and the militia stopped the rising before it began. Gabriel and 25 others were hanged.

documents.title: A church of their own
documents.source: Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.12 B. The Cultures of African-American Communities: the African Methodist Episcopal Church.
documents.sourcing: A course-book account of free Black Philadelphians founding their own denomination.
documents.text: In 1816, Richard Allen and other Black Methodist ministers in Philadelphia formed the African Methodist Episcopal Church, the first independent Black denomination in the United States. Allen, who had bought his own freedom from slavery, became its first bishop. Black Methodists had left white-led churches after Black worshippers were pulled from their knees at prayer.

documents.title: Pleading their own cause
documents.source: Freedom's Journal, first issue, March 16, 1827. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The first issue of the first Black-owned newspaper, written by its own editors to their readers.
documents.text: "We wish to plead our own cause. Too long have others spoken for us. Too long has the publick been deceived by misrepresentations, in things which concern us dearly."

documents.title: Walker’s Appeal
documents.source: David Walker, Appeal to the Coloured Citizens of the World (Boston, September 28, 1829). Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A free Black Bostonian writing to his fellow Black Americans, urging them to stay and resist.
documents.text: "Let no man of us budge one step, and let slave-holders come to beat us from our country. America is more our country, than it is the whites—we have enriched it with our blood and tears."

documents.title: Turner’s vision
documents.source: Nat Turner, speaking to Thomas R. Gray, The Confessions of Nat Turner (Baltimore, 1831). Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Turner’s words as recorded by the white lawyer who questioned him in jail; Gray shaped the published text.
documents.text: "And about this time I had a vision—and I saw white spirits and black spirits engaged in battle, and the sun was darkened—the thunder rolled in the heavens, and blood flowed in streams—and I heard a voice saying, “Such is your luck, such you are called to see, and let it come rough or smooth, you must surely bear it.”"

documents.title: Garnet’s call
documents.source: Henry Highland Garnet, “An Address to the Slaves of the United States,” National Negro Convention, Buffalo, New York, August 1843. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A Black minister addressing enslaved people through a convention that refused to endorse his call.
documents.text: "Brethren, arise, arise! Strike for your lives and liberties. Now is the day and the hour. . . . Rather die freemen than live to be slaves. Remember that you are FOUR MILLIONS!"

documents.title: A slave made a man
documents.source: Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave (1845), Chapter X. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Douglass tells how he fought back against the slave-breaker Edward Covey.
documents.text: In 1845, Frederick Douglass published his Narrative, telling how he fought the slave-breaker Edward Covey in August 1833: "You have seen how a man was made a slave; you shall see how a slave was made a man."

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which African Americans shaped the struggle against slavery, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent of Black shaping does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the growth of slavery with the cotton market, the Second Great Awakening, or the rise of white abolitionism.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing the content of at least three documents relevant to the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Quoting documents without describing what they show does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or using six without tying them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific relevant example not in the documents, such as the 1830 National Negro Convention, Maria Stewart’s lectures, or the domestic slave trade.
rubric.notEarned: A vague reference to outside knowledge with no specific example does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining how the audience, purpose, historical situation, or point of view of at least two documents shapes the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Naming a document’s author without explaining how it shapes the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for a complex argument, such as qualifying the thesis by showing where Black action changed the struggle and where slavery’s power limited it, or who acted and who was left out.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: African Americans shaped the struggle against slavery to a great extent between 1800 and 1848, leading it from inside slavery and from free Black communities, yet they did not end slavery, and their struggle met violent answers at every turn.
Context: The cotton market drove the dramatic growth of slavery, while the Second Great Awakening and white abolitionism gave the struggle new language.
Evidence for shaping: Gabriel and Turner rose against slavery; Allen built a church of his own; Russwurm and Cornish founded a Black press; Walker called Black Americans to resist at home; Garnet called the enslaved to rise; Douglass fought the slave-breaker Covey and told his own story in print.
Evidence for limits: Gabriel’s rising was stopped and Turner’s put down, both ending in hangings; Southern states tightened their laws; Garnet’s own convention refused his call.
Complexity: Black Americans shaped the struggle by acting as well as by arguing, and the harshest answers to their actions prove how much those actions were feared.
